q: How are coins designed and minted?
What is the process of coin manufacturing?
How are coin dies made?
What is a coin hub and how is it used?
What is planchet production in minting?
How does the coin striking process work?

how coins are manufactured design to finished product
a: Coin manufacturing begins with design: an artist creates the design concept, which is sculpted in clay or modeled digitally (using CAD software like FreeForm or zBrush), then reduced to the size of the coin through a pantograph or laser engraving system that cuts a master hub in tool steel. The master hub is used to create master dies (negative impressions), which in turn produce working hubs and working dies — this multi-generation process means that minor die deterioration artifacts (die cracks, die wear, polish lines) appear on coins as the die approaches replacement, and these markers help numismatists identify specific die states and varieties. Planchets (blank coin discs) are punched from rolled metal strips of precise composition and thickness, then annealed (softened by heating) and upset (a rim is raised by rotating the planchet between grooved plates), after which they are washed and dried before striking. The striking process uses a coining press that brings obverse and reverse dies together under immense pressure (typically 50-100 tons for large silver coins), with a third collar die containing the edge design or reeding, and modern presses can strike 400-750 coins per minute with automated feeding and sorting — after striking, coins are inspected by vision systems for defects, counted, and bagged or rolled for distribution.

a: The United States Mint operates four active coin-producing facilities: Philadelphia (the original mint, established 1792, producing primarily business strike circulation coins marked with P, and also manufacturing the master dies used at all mint facilities), Denver (established 1906, producing circulation coins marked with D, the largest volume producer of circulating coinage in the world), San Francisco (established 1854, producing primarily proof coins and some commemorative issues marked with S, known for the high-quality finish of its proof coinage since proof production began in 1968), and West Point (established as a bullion depository in 1937, elevated to mint status in 1988, producing bullion coins including American Eagles, commemorative coins, and special uncirculated sets marked with W). Historically significant but now closed US Mint facilities include the Charlotte Mint (1838-1861, gold coins, marked C), Dahlonega Mint (1838-1861, gold coins, marked D before the Denver Mint existed), New Orleans Mint (1838-1909, silver and gold coins, marked O), and Carson City Mint (1870-1893, produced the famous CC Morgan dollars, highly sought by collectors due to low mintages and the Wild West mystique of the Comstock Lode — coins from Carson City are among the most collected of all US mint issues).

a: The Royal Mint (London, headquartered in Llantrisant, Wales since 1968, founded over 1,100 years ago) produces all UK circulation coinage and banknotes, bullion coins (Britannia, Sovereign), and significant volumes of circulation, commemorative, and bullion coins for over 60 countries worldwide, making it one of the largest exporting mints globally. The Royal Canadian Mint (Winnipeg and Ottawa, founded 1908) is renowned for technological innovation: it produces the world's purest gold bullion coin (.99999 pure), pioneered colored circulation coins (the 2004 poppy quarter), and developed advanced security features including the MINTAX patented maple leaf security mark and radial lines technology for bullion coins. Monnaie de Paris (Paris, founded 864 AD, the world's oldest continuously operating mint institution) produces French euro coins, prestigious medals and art medals, and the French Mint's workshops and museum (Métal, chaired by the Contremaître as the historic master's workshop) remain operational, while the Perth Mint (Australia, founded 1899 as a branch of the Royal Mint, now owned by the Government of Western Australia) is famous for its Australian Kangaroo bullion coins and Lunar Series, and the Royal Australian Mint (Canberra, founded 1965) produces all of Australia's circulating coinage and is notable for its extensive commemorative dollar coin program.

q: How has minting technology evolved?
What was the screw press in coin minting?
What was the steam press in minting?
How did the hydraulic press change coin minting?
What are modern high-speed coin presses?
How has laser engraving changed die making?
What is the future of coin minting technology?
history of minting technology screw steam hydraulic press
modern high-speed presses laser engraving coin technology
a: Minting technology evolved from the ancient hammer-struck method (placing a planchet between two hand-held dies and striking the upper die with a hammer) to the screw press (15th century, Leonardo da Vinci designed one, where a large screw driven by a heavy counterweight or manpower brought the dies together with increased force, improving consistency of strike). The steam-powered coining press, pioneered by Matthew Boulton at the Soho Mint in Birmingham in the 1780s and perfected for the British Royal Mint, mechanized production and enabled the first large-scale, consistent coinage — Boulton's steam presses could produce 50-100 coins per minute with far greater force than manual methods, and his 1797 Cartwheel penny and twopence were the first machine-struck British copper coins. Modern minting relies on high-speed hydraulic and mechanical presses producing 400-750 coins per minute with computer-controlled precision, servo-driven feed systems, and automated quality control using machine vision and laser inspection at every stage — the latest technology includes laser engraving for die production (replacing hand-engraving and chemical etching with direct laser ablation that creates microscopic details for enhanced security features), additive manufacturing for prototyping dies, and advanced metallurgy for longer die life and planchet materials that produce superior strike quality at higher speeds.
